results.content: These abstractions could now be viewed as immediate while being mediated, what I call a “logic 227 of instant display.” By pointing to this historically situated conception of technical mediation, I nuance a dominant account in media theory that describes understandings of technical and broadcast media along the lines of either media “marginalism” or “generativism.” Instead, I see this logic of instant display as a new form of liveness that impacted the way the active brain could be thought as a new live brain, a brain as display. Chapter 5 is a revised and expanded version of “The Interface Is the (Art)Work: EEG-Feedback, Circuited Selves and the Rise of Real-Time Brainmedia (1964–1977).” In Brain Art: Brain-Computer Interfaces for Artistic Expression, edited by Anton Nijholt, 33-63.
